results.note: Header 'Review'; Methods give measurement only, no search or criteria; reference list (pp. 9-11): Greenwald first author 2002/2003/2007, second author of Zubieta 2000 ('male' in title, p. 11); Comer first author 2005; conclusion p. 1.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors use receptor availability (non-displaceable binding potential), an indirect measure, instead of 'occupancy', which they call misleading and not measurable directly in people except with extraordinary methods (to obtain receptor concentration and affinity); if receptor affinity and endogenous opioid levels are assumed constant, a fall in availability is proportional to a rise in occupancy. Measures taken 4 hours after the daily dose, the earliest post-dose time studied, probably reflect less than the largest fall in availability; within-day PET time courses are not feasible. There is no gold-standard definition of clinically meaningful blockade, and neither the availability needed for withdrawal suppression or blockade nor how it varies with patients, opioids and routes is known.
results.note: Wording only, no number changes: source says occupancy cannot be measured directly 'except with extraordinary methods', and gives proportionality under an assumption ('If we assume'), not as 'only if'. Rest confirmed at 2.1.1 and 2.2.1.

results.corrected_extracted: The studies reviewed enrolled people dependent on heroin who were not seeking treatment and who usually kept using between inpatient stays; the authors call generalizability to people dependent on other opioids, such as oxycodone or hydrocodone, or seeking treatment unclear. Ages were limited to 18–50; many fewer women than men took part, and the small samples gave too little statistical power to examine gender or age; people with substance use disorders other than nicotine, depressive, psychotic or anxiety disorders, pregnancy or medical conditions such as active hepatitis were excluded, and the authors say these relatively healthy volunteers do not represent patients in clinical practice. All imaging used a buprenorphine-only product; the authors cite data suggesting that buprenorphine and buprenorphine/naloxone products under the tongue have similar effects.
results.note: Hedge restored: 'data suggest' similar effects (Strain et al., 2000). Inadequate power is put down to small samples in general, not only to the few women. Paragraph locators and all other facts confirmed.

key_findings.correction: In the authors' summary of earlier human studies, buprenorphine brought on moderate to severe withdrawal in people maintained on methadone 60 mg/day, and less in people on methadone 25–30 mg/day or on heroin; citing animal and human studies, the review says that whether it precipitates withdrawal depends on the level of dependence, the opioid depended on, and the time since its last dose. (The dependence sentence is not limited to animal studies: it cites Kosten and Kleber, 1988, and Walsh et al., 1995a, human studies by their titles, as well as Sell et al., 2003, and Woods' animal work.)

Finding unchanged and confirmed; note corrected to: Availability is the share of receptors still free to bind the tracer; the authors treat a fall in availability as proportional to a rise in occupancy if receptor affinity and endogenous opioid levels are assumed constant (2.1.1, PDF p. 3). The legend of Fig. 1 gives 12–33% for 8 mg/day, against 20–35% in Table 1 (see reporting issues). (The source says 'proportional', under an assumption, not 'equate ... only if'.)

reporting_issues.correction: issue: Table 1, note b, says that values for doses not studied are in italics, but no value in Table 1 is italicized (checked on the page rendered at 300 dpi); only the text and the data points of Fig. 1 (left panel) show that 2, 16 and 32 mg/day were studied. The 1 mg/day estimate lies below the studied range (2–32 mg/day), and the text calls the range of estimates 16-fold although the table spans 1 to 32 mg/day. | consequence: Curve-fit estimates (1, 4, 8, 12 and 24 mg/day) can be mistaken for measurements; the 1 mg/day value is an extrapolation.

risk_of_bias.note: Narrative review, no applicable instrument; overall high and the five domains are supported by the PDF (no search; authors' own studies; abstract states thresholds the Summary calls preliminary).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: abstract gives thresholds and dose translations as results; 2.2.1 says the thresholds are unknown and 4.3 says blockade not reliably observed and the 20% figure is preliminary modelling.

missed: outcomes.validity_norms says a fall in availability 'equals' a rise in occupancy 'only if' affinity and endogenous levels stay constant, and that occupancy 'cannot be measured directly in humans'; the source (2.1.1, PDF p. 3) says 'proportional', under an assumption, and adds 'except with extraordinary methods' (receptor concentration and affinity).

Source inconsistency not flagged: 2.2.3, 7th paragraph (PDF p. 4) says all imaging studies used a BUP-mono tablet, but Results, 1st paragraph (p. 4) says Zubieta et al. (2000) used the liquid formulation; sample.selection_effects repeats 'tablet' while the card's exposure field says liquid.

Results, 7th paragraph (PDF p. 5) and Fig. 3 upper left (p. 6): in the 2003 study, availability related to withdrawal and craving but the effects were 'clinically modest' (<50% of maximum effect); in the figure withdrawal stays below about 30% of maximum even at placebo (read from the plot), which bears on the ≤50% withdrawal-suppression threshold.
